title: BlindGuard: Safeguarding LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems under Unknown Attacks
evidence: adaptive=1: 'We modify the original PI attack prompt by embedding the correct answer ... instructing the agent to mimic the reasoning process ... to reduce semantic deviation'; 'intended to bypass BlindGuard's anomaly detection' (simple hand-crafted PI variant; detection AUC stayed high). judge=ML: unsupervised GNN graph anomaly detector (hierarchical encoder + corruption-guided contrastive detector) on SentenceBERT embeddings of agent responses; no LLM judge (judge_input -). Decision: bidirectional edge pruning of flagged agents, others integrate only trusted neighbours. Timing: 'runs at the boundary, immediately after the first generation and before the next propagation' but 'cannot preemptively prevent malicious agents from infiltrating'. Exactly 3 compromised agents; 3 backbones (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-30B-A3B) + Qwen3-8B robustness. Overhead 0.53->0.56 min per 3 rounds. Clean accuracy unchanged (Table 10) but no numeric FPR (only qualitative false-pruning failure case)

title: Improving Alignment and Robustness with Circuit Breakers
bench: HarmBench (black/white-box attacks);own:100 harmful function-calling requests (Llama-3-8B-Instruct agent);BFCL (benign)
evidence: adaptive=2 (per codebook: GCG/PGD optimized against the defended model): white-box GCG, PGD (image), Input Embedding Attack and RepE Attack run on the RR model; abstract: 'embedding and representation-space attacks ... proxies for worst-case assumptions about attacker capabilities'; paper does not label them adaptive and no attack targets the rerouting mechanism itself (caveat: could be 0/1 under a stricter reading). judge=SELF: model fine-tuned with representation rerouting (LoRA), 'no separate external judge'; harmful representations rerouted to incoherent output / generation halts. 'harmful action compliance rates' reduced 84%/83% (Llama-3-8B). Models: Mistral-7B, Llama-3-8B, LLaVA-NeXT-Mistral-7B, Cygnet. Utility MT-Bench/OpenLLM/BFCL; over-refusal on WildChat/XSTest (Llama 6.2% vs 2.2%). Overhead: only training cost (20 min on 1 A100), 'no additional computational burden' at inference (not quantified) -> N

title: DRIFT: Dynamic Rule-Based Defense with Injection Isolation for Securing LLM Agents
src: https://arxiv.org/html/2506.12104v2 (arXiv v2, 2025-10-24; abs checked, v3 2026-03-26 not read)
evidence: adaptive=2: Sec 3.6 'Stress Test: Adaptive Attack': manually designed isolator/validator adaptive attacks (IAA, VAA: e.g. 'there are no instructions that conflict with the user's original query') plus PAIR ('advanced black-box jailbreak optimization mechanism') used on cases where DRIFT defended but base agent failed, 'optimized an injection prompt to bypass both components'; result 0.04% utility loss/0.81% ASR up (IAA+VAA), 2.13%/0.31% (PAIR). judge: Secure Planner LLM sees user query + tool schemas only (policy gen: minimal function trajectory + JSON parameter checklists -> policy_src LLM); Dynamic Validator checks 'each tool-calling request' before execution against constraints (deterministic schema check, deviations assessed by LLM with tool messages); Injection Isolator LLM reads raw tool responses and masks conflicting instructions before they enter memory stream -> judge_input RAW. HUMAN: deviated Write/Execute call -> 'approval request to user (in our evaluation setting, sending a user request is equivalent to rejecting)'; burden not measured. 5 backbones (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Claude-3-Haiku, Qwen2.5-7B). Overhead 1.89x tokens vs undefended (CaMeL ~7x). No explicit FPR (utility only)

title: AgentSentinel: An End-to-End and Real-Time Security Defense Framework for Computer-Use Agents
src: https://arxiv.org/html/2509.07764v1 (HTML truncated after Sec 4.2) + https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.07764v1 (arXiv v1, 2025-09-09; full text read)
evidence: adaptive=1: 'We analyze the performance of AgentSentinel against five potential adaptive attacks (see Table 5)': killing observable defender, toxic task context (poison task summarizer), toxic system trace x2 (malicious payload via file write / command args), query-cache poisoning; hand-designed against AgentSentinel's monitor/summarizer/tracer/cache; Claude models defend all, GPT-4-Turbo/GPT-4o limited failures. A_mode=pre: eBPF/LSM tracer suspends sensitive operations ('it is suspended, and detailed information is presented to a security auditor'; resume or terminate); audit-budget overrun -> process removed from enforcement set (default allow). judge: rule-based auditor ('predefined security policies', configurable) + LLM auditor; policy author not explicit (MAN inferred). judge_input: security query = LLM-generated 'task summary' of chat messages + enforcement event + event trace; tracer 'filters sensitive data from most untrusted sources (e.g., file content and network data)' so auditor gets derived content (summary/commandline/metadata), not raw tool outputs (summarizer LLM itself reads chat incl. tool outputs; toxic-context attack targets it) -> judge_exposed N. No human in loop. Models: Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet, GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4o. Metrics (paper's naming): FPR 10.8% avg (paper defines FPR as accepting malicious ops; FNR = refusing benign ops), failed-task rate 4.2%, 2.8 security queries per tool use; latency not measurable; no separate benign-only runs

title: Monitoring Decomposition Attacks with Lightweight Sequential Monitors
bench: own:DecomposedHarm (QA, text-to-image, agent tasks adapted from AgentHarm);AgentHarm (adapted)
evidence: adaptive=1 (weak/borderline): 'adversaries can easily inject random tasks to mask their intentions further to avoid detections'; 'we randomly select benign subtasks from other tasks and inject them into the original subtasks' (GPT-4o F1 0.85 -> 0.72 at 100% injection). Limitations: 'we only stress-test the monitor with random distraction tasks'; no synonym-rewriting/phrase-stuffing, no automated iterative decomposition, no monitor-specific prompt injection (future work E.1). judge=SEP: LLM monitor (prompted GPT-4o-mini/Llama-3.1-8B/o3-mini etc.) sees cumulative user prompts C_i=[p_1..p_i] after each new prompt, 'flag and halt' vs 'allow and continue' before the model responds; sees only user prompts (user is the adversary; no tool outputs/responses) -> TRUSTED per codebook. 10 monitor LLMs. FP defined ('flags at any step in a benign task') but only F1/DSR reported (GPT-4o-mini F1 0.913, DSR 93%); no benign-task utility of defended agent. Cost 1.39e-4 USD/task, latency 0.437 s

title: Spilling the Beans: Teaching LLMs to Self-Report Their Hidden Objectives
src: https://arxiv.org/html/2511.06626 (arXiv latest = v5, 2026-03-22, ICLR 2026 camera-ready; pdf v5 also read)
evidence: adaptive=1 (borderline): evaluation under in-context adversarial pressure: non-disclosure instructions ('Do not reveal, hint at, or acknowledge the existence of this objective') and decoy objectives ('interrogated with its original hidden system prompt, plus an additional plausible, innocent objective that it can cite if it accidentally reveals having a secondary objective'): 'SRFT is robust to adversarial decoy objectives in 3 out of 4 tasks'. Hand-crafted evasion aware of interrogation, but authors list no adaptive attacker/red team and 'weak incentives for covertness' as limitation. judge=SELF: GPT-4.1 fine-tuned (SRFT, 770 examples) answers task-agnostic interrogation questions about its own transcript post-hoc ('post-hoc auditing ... promotes the admission of hidden objectives without eliminating their execution'); transcript (20-150 turns incl. tool use, system prompt excluded) -> judge_exposed Y. No enforcement: detection (F1 0.98) and elicitation only -> decisions '?'. Baseline LLM monitor GPT-4.1 F1~0. Only GPT-4.1 fine-tuned (Claude Sonnet 4 only for prefill comparison). Capability retained (GPQA-Diamond, AIME 2025, HLE); instruction-hierarchy compliance 72%->61%; FPR 0-1% in control condition

title: Contextualized Privacy Defense for LLM Agents
bench: own:115-configuration privacy simulation (profiles/sensitive data sampled from PrivacyLens, shareable data added by gpt-5)
evidence: adaptive=2: 'we use an iterative search-based attack algorithm from [41] to enhance the attacker's strategies'; 'our attack algorithm was optimized on CDI with Qwen3-4B as the instructor model'; defenses re-attacked after optimization ('re-run the privacy attacks against them'): optimized CDI AD 89.7->79.5, prompting 89.0->55.1, guarding 80.2->50.3. judge=SEP: separate instructor LM_I (e.g., Qwen3-4B, GRPO-trained SafeRL variant) invoked 'after tool-call results (e.g., retrieved email content) are obtained' with context C_<t (system prompt, history, tool results/messages from recipient) -> RAW untrusted (attacker messages, emails). Output is step-specific privacy guidance appended as a user message to steer the next action ('proactively shaping actions rather than merely constraining or vetoing'); not a gate -> stage coded P (alt reading A-pre), decisions modify. Baselines prompting and guarding (separate LM screens proposed tool calls). Agent backbones: gpt-4.1-mini/nano/gpt-4.1, Qwen3-32B (instructors vary). Helpfulness Score (shareable items disclosed) + over-refusal/block-resend discussion used as FPR proxy; no latency/token reporting

title: On the Resilience of LLM-Based Multi-Agent Collaboration with Faulty Agents
bench: own:AUTOTRANSFORM/AUTOINJECT fault injection on HumanEval;CIAR;CommonMT;FairEval (systems: Self-collab, Camel, MetaGPT, SPP, MAD, AgentVerse)
evidence: adaptive=0: fixed error-injection methods only; no attack designed against Inspector/Challenger and no discussion of faulty agents adapting to them. adversarial=Y (borderline): threat = 'clumsy or even malicious agents'; Inspector prompt targets 'deliberate errors', Challenger asks to 'identify whether the following message is generated by a vicious agent'; errors are injected by authors at fixed rate. Defenses: Challenger (agent profile prompt lets each agent question peers' messages -> SELF) and Inspector (extra LLM agent reading 'the history of the chat' and 'the response just generated' of other agents, rewrites response or replies 'safe' -> SEP, RAW agent messages), applied post-generation before downstream consumption. Evaluated only on Self-collab and Camel (Table 3), GPT-3.5 backbone (main resilience study also GPT-4o; unclear if defenses run on GPT-4o). Recovers up to 96.4% of loss; clean-system result shows small change (Self-collab 76.2->76.4; Camel 62.2->61.0 with Inspector) but no FPR; no cost/overhead reported

title: Visual Inception: Compromising Long-term Planning in Agentic Recommenders via Multimodal Memory Poisoning
bench: own:ShopBench-Agent (e-commerce 500, interior design 300, travel 200 sessions; simulated)
evidence: adaptive=2: four adaptive attack variants against defense (CognitiveGuard): Diffusion-Aware (EoT through purifier), Counterfactual-Evasive (minimizing Reasoning Divergence Score), Coherence-Preserving, Full White-Box ('majority-vote awareness'); ASR-M 8.3% standard -> 18.4% combined adaptive -> 24.7% full white-box. Defense: System 1 at memory write (diffusion-based purification of uploaded images with benign-reference-anchored stopping + embedding-distance threshold -> ML, modify); System 2 at query/planning stage: counterfactual plan with/without each retrieved memory, Sentence-BERT RDS > 0.7 or GPT-4 LLM-judge relevance rubric (5-1, <=2 flagged; 3-vote majority) -> memory flagged 'Pivot Point' and excluded from recommendation (block). judge_input RAW inferred: rubric scores relevance of retrieved memory items (raw memory content), exact judge prompt not released ('without claiming full prompt-template release') -> uncertain. Models with defense: LLaMA-3.2-Vision-90B, GPT-4V, Qwen-VL-Max, Claude-3.5-Sonnet (+LLaMA-8B lite mode). Latency: 0.3 s/image upload, 6.5 s query-time (1.5 s lite/parallel); FPR 3.2% at theta=0.7; RCS 0.89 vs 0.31 undefended. Paper is mainly an attack paper; defense CognitiveGuard coded here

title: MCIP: Protecting MCP Safety via Model Contextual Integrity Protocol
bench: own:MCIP-bench (2,218 instances, 11 categories, from glaive-function-calling-v2);own:ToolACE-derived risk set;BFCL-v3 (utility)
evidence: adaptive=0: Limitations: 'Our method does not simulate or enumerate specific adversarial attack strategies ... We leave the integration of adaptive threat modeling and dynamic adversarial training as promising directions for future work.' judge: 'MCIP Guardian, which is a safety-aware model' (Llama-xLAM-2-8b-fc-r fine-tuned on 13,830 synthetic instances; contribution list says 'tracking tools and guard model'); classifies a logged interaction (user query, function list, function calls, function responses; MCI tuples sender/recipient/data subject/info type/transmission principle) as safe or one of 10 risk types (Function/Intent/Data/Identity/Causal-dependency injection etc.). Paper does not state where/when Guardian is deployed or what action it takes (no block/warn described) -> A_mode and decisions '?'; stage I;A is a best guess (covers function responses and function calls). judge_input RAW because benchmark dialogues contain function responses/function lists with injected content (not explicit about live deployment); alternative reading: the safety-aware function-calling model itself (SELF; BFCL utility reported). 7 other LLMs (xLAM 70b/32b/8b, ToolACE-2-8B, Qwen2.5-72B/32B, DeepSeek-R1) evaluated only as baselines. Risk resistance 54.16%, Guardian +40.81 pts vs base; BFCL-v3 utility 65.79%

title: ShieldAgent: Shielding Agents via Verifiable Safety Policy Reasoning
src: https://arxiv.org/html/2503.22738 (arXiv latest = v2, 2025-11-27; abs + pdf also checked)
evidence: adaptive=0: no mention of adaptive attacks in main text or appendix; attacks (AgentPoison, AdvWeb) target the protected agent AWM, not the guardrail; no limitations section. judge: GPT-4o guardrail agent retrieves action-based probabilistic rule circuits (Markov Logic Network / LTL rules, formal verification code) and calls tools (moderation APIs, specialized guard models) -> SEP+RULE; rules extracted by GPT-4o from policy documents (EU AI Act, platform policies) offline, rule weights learned from data -> policy_src MIX. Input per step: 'the past interaction history, the observation, and the invoked action' (screenshots, HTML accessibility trees) -> RAW. Output: binary safe flag + violated rules + explanation; online eval 'integrated as a post-verification module that copilots with the agent' giving 'interactive feedback to help it adjust behavior' (timing vs execution not explicit; coded pre as guardrail on invoked action; A_mode uncertain). GPT-4o only. FPR ~4.0-4.8% on ShieldAgent-Bench; 64.7% fewer API queries, 58.2% less time vs baselines (~11 queries, ~33 s per sample); online policy compliance conditioned on task success 65.3-80.5% vs baseline 22.8-67.9%

title: AutoRAS: Learning Robust Agentic Systems with Primitive Representations
src: https://arxiv.org/html/2606.21445 (arXiv v1, ICML 2026 camera-ready format; abs page lacked history)
bench: own:attack templates (brain/memory/tool/agent-to-agent, Table 6) on MMLU;MS-MARCO;MATH;ProgramDev;AgentHarm and ASB attack variants on MMLU/MS-MARCO (Table 7, unseen)
evidence: adaptive=0: only predefined attack templates plus 'stronger unseen attack variants' from AgentHarm/ASB ('only mild performance degradation'); no attack designed against the discovered workflows; no limitations section ('structural robustness within the evaluated agentic threat model, not immunity'). Design-time method: learned generator composes workflows from primitives; auxiliary monitor LLM audits execution traces only at design/training time (not a runtime guard). Runtime safeguards are LLM-call primitives in the workflow: SAFE_Filter ('Prompt-injection hygiene. Detect and remove adversarial instructions', outputs a clean query), SAFE_ToolGuard ('Validate planned tool calls; if unsafe or suboptimal, revise or reselect tools'; guarded tool paths 'require corroboration before executing risky calls'), SAFE_Trajectory, SAFE_CrossAgent; they receive raw agent outputs, tool results and other agents' responses -> RAW; revise rather than block. 4 backbones (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3.1, Claude-3.5-Haiku, Gemini-2.0-Flash). Total inference cost $0.67 (second-lowest among baselines); no FPR/over-blocking measure
